title: Nora’s Lesion in a Child: A Case of Complete Spontaneous Regression
content: We describe a complete spontaneous regression of the Nora’s lesion of the first metatarsal in a 3-year-old child with hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type IV (HSNA IV) with congenital insensitivity to pain and anhidrosis. The patient presented at our clinic with a non-tender mass in the dorsal region of the foot. No history of trauma was reported. The skin above the lesion was slightly warm without local bruising. Routine laboratory examinations were unremarkable, except for an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 6.13 mg/dL (normal range, <0.5 mg/dL).X-ray scan and magnetic resonance imaging of the foot revealed a calcified mass adjacent to the cortical surface of the first metatarsal bone (Figure 1). The imaging findings were not specific; therefore, biopsy was performed to achieve an accurate histological diagnosis. Possible differential diagnoses included bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation (known as Nora’s lesion), periosteal chondroma, osteochondroma, osteomyelitis, myositis ossificans, and parosteal osteosarcoma. Histological examination revealed a diagnosis of Nora’s lesion (Figure 2), and intraoperative microbiological examinations were negative for infection. Considering the very young age of the patient, the benign nature of the lesion, and the high recurrence rates (55%) reported in the literature (1), we decided to follow a “wait and see” protocol. Surgical treatment would have been considered only in case of an increase in the lesion size. Although an evident source of infection was not found and the blood cultures were negative, an intravenous antibiotic therapy (ceftriaxone, 50 mg/kg/day) was started to prevent infection that represents one of the possible complications related to HSNA IV (2). The therapy was continued for 7 days, achieving normalization of the CRP level that remained negative even at the follow-up after 4 and 8 weeks of the antibiotic therapy. We evaluated the patient every 6 months with a clinical and radiological assessment. Surprisingly, the X-ray imaging performed during the follow-up showed a progressive remission of the lesion with complete regression within 2 years (Figure 1).In this report, we present a pediatric case of a Nora’s lesion that showed a progressive, spontaneous, and complete regression. The choice of a “wait and see” approach with clinical and radiological evaluation every 6 months proved to be successful, and a preventive antibiotic therapy avoided any infective complications. Surgical treatment remained an option to be considered only in case of an increase of the lesion size, which did not occur. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first case reported in literature in which Nora’s lesion regressed spontaneously (3). This peculiarity makes it original and may support the theory that the Nora’s lesion may be a reactive process. In contrast, recent studies have reported some chromosomal anomalies associated with this entity, whose etiopathology remains to be completely understood (4, 5).

diagnosis.diagnosis_raw: Nora’s lesion of the first metatarsal in a 3-year-old child with hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type IV (HSNA IV) with congenital insensitivity to pain and anhidrosis.
diagnosis.disease_name: Nora’s lesion (bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation) of the first metatarsal
diagnosis.severity_description: Benign calcified mass adjacent to the cortical surface of the first metatarsal; progressive spontaneous regression reported
diagnosis.lab_values: CRP 6.13 mg/dL (normal <0.5 mg/dL); normalized after antibiotics; blood cultures negative.
diagnosis.disease_duration_before_healing: Complete regression within 2 years (progressive remission on follow-up imaging).
diagnosis.primary_site: First metatarsal (foot), adjacent to cortical surface

treatment.treatments_raw: ‘Wait and see’ protocol with clinical and radiological evaluation every 6 months; preventive intravenous antibiotic therapy (ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg/day) for 7 days.
treatment.treatment_stopped_reason: Antibiotic prophylaxis completed after 7 days; surgery deferred unless lesion increased.

remission_outcome.verification_detail: Initial diagnosis supported by X-ray and MRI; biopsy/histology confirmed Nora’s lesion; serial follow-up X-rays every 6 months showed progressive remission with complete regression within 2 years.
remission_outcome.biomarker_trajectory: CRP 6.13 mg/dL → normalized after 7 days ceftriaxone; remained negative at 4- and 8-week follow-up.
remission_outcome.follow_up_duration_raw: Follow-up every 6 months; complete regression within 2 years

pre_illness_state.patient_causal_belief: Authors suggest the lesion may be a reactive process; etiopathology not fully understood.

validation.statistical_improbability_notes: Authors state this is the first reported case in the literature of spontaneous regression of Nora’s lesion.
validation.extraction_notes: Remission is radiographically documented over 2 years; lesion is benign (not terminal). Antibiotics were given prophylactically for HSNA IV-related infection risk, but remission is described as spontaneous.

analysis.case_summary: A 3-year-old child with HSNA IV had a biopsy-confirmed Nora’s lesion adjacent to the first metatarsal. Managed with observation and short-course prophylactic IV ceftriaxone, serial X-rays showed progressive spontaneous regression with complete radiographic resolution within 2 years.
key_healing_factors: Observation ('wait and see') with serial clinical and radiological follow-up
No surgical intervention; lesion regressed progressively on imaging
Short prophylactic IV ceftriaxone with normalization of elevated CRP (infection not identified)
unique_features: First reported spontaneous regression of Nora’s lesion per authors
Very young pediatric patient (age 3) with HSNA IV (congenital insensitivity to pain and anhidrosis)
Biopsy/histology confirmation with serial radiographic documentation of complete regression
analysis.analysis_notes: This is a benign musculoskeletal proliferative lesion rather than cancer. Remission is described as spontaneous and complete, verified by serial X-rays, with initial MRI and biopsy confirmation. Antibiotic therapy addressed elevated CRP/prophylaxis rather than a proven infection; its relationship to lesion regression is unclear from the narrative.
